# BrassCoders Research Index — llms.txt

> AI-readable context for the BrassCoders research repository.
> For AI agents, search engines, and LLM tooling.

## What this repository is

This repository is the research evidence base for BrassCoders, a static-analysis CLI that scans AI-generated Python code for security vulnerabilities, performance anti-patterns, and supply-chain risks.

The repository contains:
- 17 research categories organized around developer questions
- 97 primary sources: academic papers, industry reports, company disclosures, open-source tools, and benchmark corpora
- Machine-readable index at data/research.json
- Full source annotations explaining what BrassCoders draws from each source

Sources last verified August 2026.

## BrassCoders (the product)

- **What it is:** A Python CLI (`pip install brasscoders`) that runs 12 static-analysis scanners against any Python codebase and emits findings as YAML formatted for AI coding assistants (Claude Code, Cursor, Continue).
- **Why it exists:** AI coding assistants generate code with a structural rate of security bugs, performance anti-patterns, and supply-chain risks. BrassCoders is the deterministic detection layer that complements AI generation.
- **License:** Apache 2.0 (OSS core). Paid enrichment tier available at $12/dev/month.
- **OSS repo:** github.com/CopperSunDev/brasscoders
- **Product site:** coppersun.dev

## Research categories (17)

1. cve-risk — Will My AI-Generated Code Ship A CVE? (12 sources)
   Lead finding: Veracode State of Software Security 2026: 45% of AI-generated code samples introduce at least one OWASP Top 10 vulnerability on first generation

2. slopsquatting — Will My AI Hallucinate An Import? (6 sources)
   Lead finding: USENIX Security 2025: 19.7% of AI-recommended packages do not exist on the relevant registry across major models

3. cross-file-bugs — Why Does My AI Miss Cross-File Bugs? (5 sources)
   Lead finding: Lost in the Middle (Liu et al. 2023, Stanford / Berkeley) documents LLM attention decay: models reliably attend to the start and end of long inputs and lose attention through the middle — the structural proof that larger context windows do not close the cross-file bug gap

4. llm-review-reliability — How Reliable Is My AI Assistant's Review? (7 sources)
   Lead finding: Amro & Alalfi (2025) found Copilot's code review feature frequently fails to detect critical vulnerabilities including SQL injection, cross-site scripting, and insecure deserialization, concentrating instead on low-severity style and formatting issues

5. market-intelligence — What Does The AI-Coding Market Look Like In 2026? (6 sources)
   Lead finding: Gartner projects 75-90% of enterprise software engineers will use AI code assistants by 2028, up from approximately 14% in early 2024

6. performance-anti-patterns — Will My AI Write Slow Code? (7 sources)
   Lead finding: BrassCoders AI-coder-bugs corpus: on twelve AI-generated Python files, BrassCoders caught all four planted performance anti-patterns while Bandit, Semgrep, and Pylint each caught none

7. secret-leakage — Will My AI-Generated Code Leak My Credentials? (4 sources)
   Lead finding: GitGuardian State of Secrets Sprawl 2024 found over 12.8 million secrets exposed in public GitHub commits in a single year

8. dependency-confusion — Will My AI Mix Up Internal and Public Packages? (4 sources)
   Lead finding: Birsan 2021 demonstrated dependency confusion against 35 organizations — Apple, Microsoft, PayPal, Netflix, Shopify, Tesla, and Uber among them — with total bug bounty payouts exceeding $130,000

9. weak-crypto — Will My AI Use Weak Crypto? (5 sources)
   Lead finding: Pearce et al. (IEEE S&P 2022): approximately 40% of 1,689 GitHub Copilot programs vulnerable across 89 CWE-Top-25 scenarios, with CWE-327 cryptography scenarios among the worst-handled

10. prompt-injection — Can My AI Coding Agent Be Hijacked? (5 sources)
   Lead finding: Liu et al. 2025 ("Your AI, My Shell"): AIShellJack framework of 314 payloads across 70 MITRE ATT&CK techniques; up to 84% attack success executing malicious commands on GitHub Copilot and Cursor

11. vibe-coding-velocity-risk — What Does Coding At AI Speed Do To Security And Quality? (3 sources)
   Lead finding: Andrej Karpathy coined vibe coding in February 2025: fully AI-driven authorship where the developer vibe-checks rather than reads the output

12. agentic-ai-code-security — How Do I Secure Code That AI Agents Write Autonomously, Or Code That Uses Agents? (4 sources)
   Lead finding: SWE-bench (Jimenez, Yang et al. 2024): canonical benchmark for autonomous coding agents; 2,294 real GitHub issues from 12 Python repositories; measures pass rate on existing test suites

13. ai-code-regulated-industries — What Do HIPAA, GDPR, SOC 2, And Other Regulations Require When AI Writes Your Code? (4 sources)
   Lead finding: NIST AI RMF 1.0 (January 2023): US federal baseline for AI risk governance; GOVERN 1.7 requires documentation of AI system capabilities, limitations, and known failure modes

14. access-control-idor — Will My AI-Generated API Let One User See Another User's Data? (5 sources)
   Lead finding: OWASP Top 10 2021: Broken Access Control moved from fifth place in 2017 to first in 2021, present in 94% of tested applications, with 318,487 total occurrences across 34 mapped CWEs and 19,013 CVEs tied to the category

15. insecure-deserialization — Will My AI Use pickle.load Or yaml.load On Untrusted Data? (8 sources)
   Lead finding: CWE-502 (MITRE): Deserialization of Untrusted Data — the canonical taxonomy for pickle, yaml.load, and model-loading vulnerabilities, with gadget-chain attacks as the exploitation mechanism

16. code-provenance-license-risk — Does My AI-Generated Code Carry Hidden License Risk? (5 sources)
   Lead finding: Carlini et al. (ICLR 2022, "Quantifying Memorization Across Neural Language Models"): memorization in language models scales log-linearly with model capacity, training-data duplication count, and prompt context length

17. redos-resource-exhaustion — Will My AI Write A Regex That Hangs My Server? (7 sources)
   Lead finding: CWE-1333 defines ReDoS as a regular expression whose worst-case complexity is inefficient and possibly exponential in input length; also known as catastrophic backtracking

## Key sources

- Veracode State of Software Security 2026: 45% of AI-generated code samples introduce at least one OWASP Top 10 vulnerability on first generation.
- Cloud Security Alliance 2026: a near-sixfold increase in CVEs attributed to AI-generated code within a single quarter (6 in January 2026 to 35 in March 2026).
- USENIX Security 2025: 19.7% of AI-recommended packages do not exist on the relevant registry.
- Lasso Security PoC: a hallucinated huggingface-cli package received over 30,000 downloads.
- GitGuardian State of Secrets Sprawl 2024: over 12.8 million secrets exposed in public GitHub commits in a single year.
- Birsan 2021 dependency confusion: worked against 35 organizations with bug bounty payouts exceeding $130,000.
- Gartner: 75-90% of enterprise engineers projected to use AI code assistants by 2028.

## What BrassCoders is not

- BrassCoders is not an SCA (software composition analysis) tool — it does not scan package versions for known CVEs
- BrassCoders does not perform DAST (dynamic analysis)
- BrassCoders does not scan infrastructure or deployment configuration
- BrassCoders does not provide AI-based inference of context — it is a deterministic pattern reporter, not a smart reviewer
